sections.text: This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

In this Sanhita: (a) bailable offence means an offence shown as bailable in the First Schedule; (b) non-bailable offence means any other offence; (c) cognizable offence means an offence for which a police officer may arrest without warrant.
There shall be the following classes of Criminal Courts: Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the First Class, Judicial Magistrates of the Second Class, Executive Magistrates.
The State Government shall establish a Court of Session for every sessions division.
In every district, there shall be Courts of Judicial Magistrates of the First Class.
The High Court shall appoint a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class to be the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
The State Government may appoint Executive Magistrates and shall appoint one as the District Magistrate.
The State Government shall appoint a Public Prosecutor for every district.

sections.section_title: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass
sections.text: (1) The High Court may pass any sentence authorised by law. (2) A Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge may pass any sentence authorised by law; but any sentence of death passed by any such Judge shall be subject to confirmation by the High Court.

(1) The Court of a Chief Judicial Magistrate may pass any sentence authorised by law except a sentence of death or of imprisonment for life or of imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years. (2) The Court of a Magistrate of the first class may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or of fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, or of both, or of community service. (3) The Court of Magistrate of the second class may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or of fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees, or of both, or of community service.

sections.section_title: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine
sections.text: (1) The Court of a Magistrate may award such term of imprisonment in default of payment of fine as is authorised by law: Provided that the term (a) is not in excess of the powers of the Magistrate under section 23; (b) shall not, where imprisonment has been awarded as part of the substantive sentence, exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which the Magistrate is competent to inflict. (2) The imprisonment awarded under this section may be in addition to a substantive sentence of imprisonment for the maximum term awardable by the Magistrate under section 23.

sections.section_title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial
sections.text: (1) When a person is convicted at one trial of two or more offences, the Court may sentence him for such offences to the several punishments prescribed therefor which such Court is competent to inflict and shall order such punishments to run concurrently or consecutively. (2) In the case of consecutive sentences, it shall not be necessary for the Court to send the offender for trial before a higher Court: Provided that (a) in no case shall such person be sentenced to imprisonment for a longer period than twenty years; (b) the aggregate punishment shall not exceed twice the amount of punishment which the Court is competent to inflict for a single offence.

sections.section_title: Powers of superior officers of police
sections.text: Police officers superior in rank to an officer in charge of a police station may exercise the same powers, throughout the local area to which they are appointed, as may be exercised by such officer within the limits of his station.
sections.chapter: IV — Powers of Superior Officers of Police

sections.section_title: Public when to assist Magistrates and police
sections.text: Every person is bound to assist a Magistrate or police officer reasonably demanding his aid (a) in the taking or preventing the escape of any other person whom such Magistrate or police officer is authorised to arrest; or (b) in the prevention or suppression of a breach of the peace; or (c) in the prevention of any injury attempted to be committed to any public property.
sections.chapter: IV — Powers of Superior Officers of Police

sections.section_title: Public to give information of certain offences
sections.text: Every person, aware of the commission of, or of the intention of any other person to commit, any offence punishable under certain specified sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 shall, in the absence of any reasonable excuse, forthwith give information to the nearest Magistrate or police officer of such commission or intention.
sections.chapter: IV — Powers of Superior Officers of Police

sections.text: Any police officer may arrest any person concerned in a cognizable offence without a warrant.
A police officer shall not arrest for a non-cognizable offence except under a warrant.

sections.section_title: Arrest on information of design to commit cognizable offence
sections.text: A police officer may arrest without warrant if it appears a person is about to commit a cognizable offence.
A police officer may arrest upon requisition of another police officer.
A Magistrate may arrest any person for an offence committed in his presence.
Any private person may arrest any person who commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence in his presence.
A police officer making an arrest shall touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested.
The police officer may search the arrested person.
Search of a woman shall be made by another woman.
Every arrested person shall be informed of the grounds of arrest.

sections.section_title: Right to be produced before Magistrate
sections.text: Every arrested person shall be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours.
Every arrested person has the right to meet, consult, and be defended by an advocate.
When arrested without warrant for a bailable offence, the police officer shall release on bail.

sections.section_title: Notice to appear instead of arrest
sections.text: A police officer may issue a notice to appear instead of arrest for bailable offences.
When any person who is bound by any bond taken under this Sanhita to appear before a Court, does not appear, the Court may issue a warrant for his arrest and may order his property to be attached.
A Judicial Magistrate may at any time issue a warrant for the arrest of any person who has committed an offence in his presence and may order the arrest of any such person.

Any police officer may, without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant, arrest any person who has been concerned in any cognizable offence, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists of his having been so concerned.

sections.section_title: Arrest on refusal to give name and residence
sections.text: When any person who is accused of a non-cognizable offence refuses to give his name and residence, or gives a name or residence which the police officer has reason to believe to be false, he may be arrested by such police officer.

sections.section_title: Arrest of deserter from armed forces
sections.text: Any police officer may arrest a person who is a deserter from the armed forces of the Union.

sections.section_title: Arrest by private person and procedure on such arrest
sections.text: Any private person may arrest any person who in his presence commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence, or who is a proclaimed offender, and shall without unnecessary delay make over the person so arrested to a police officer.

sections.section_title: Arrest by magistrate's order or by police officer in certain cases
sections.text: When any person is arrested by any police officer under a warrant, the police officer shall inform the person arrested of the substance of the warrant and shall, if required, show him the warrant.

In making an arrest, the police officer or other person making the same shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody by word or action.

sections.section_title: Search of place entered by person sought to be arrested
sections.text: If any person acting under a warrant of arrest, or any police officer who may arrest without warrant, has reason to believe that the person to be arrested has entered into or is within any place, the person residing in or being in charge of such place shall allow him free ingress thereto and afford all reasonable facilities for a search therein.
A Magistrate may issue a search warrant if he has reason to believe evidence is in a person's possession.
A Magistrate may issue a search warrant for any wrongfully confined person.
A police officer may search without warrant for anything connected with a cognizable offence.

sections.section_title: Search of place entered by person sought to be arrested
sections.text: If a police officer has reason to believe that a person to be arrested has entered a place, the occupier of the place shall allow free ingress for search.

sections.section_title: Power to break open door or window
sections.text: A police officer may break open any outer or inner door or window of any house in order to liberate himself or any other person who is detained therein.

sections.section_title: Power to search for person wrongfully confined
sections.text: If any Magistrate has reason to believe that a person is wrongfully confined, he may issue a warrant to search for the person so confined.
If a Magistrate has reason to believe that any property is stolen or secreted, he may issue a warrant to search for it.
The officer shall call two or more independent residents to witness the search.
Every search warrant shall be directed to one or more police officers, or to any other person named therein.
A police officer may seize property suspected to be stolen or used as evidence.
A police officer may, without a warrant, search any place for the purpose of investigation if he has reason to believe that anything necessary for the investigation may be found there.
Any officer in charge of a police station may investigate any cognizable offence.

Any police officer in charge of a police station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable offence which a Court having jurisdiction over the local area within the limits of such station would have power to inquire into or try.

sections.section_title: Procedure where investigation cannot be completed
sections.text: If upon information of the commission of a cognizable offence, the officer in charge of a police station has reason to suspect the commission of such offence, he shall forthwith send a report to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of such offence.
A police officer making an investigation may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any person who appears to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case.

A police officer making an investigation may examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case, and shall reduce into writing any statement made by the person so examined.

sections.section_title: When police may arrest without warrant
sections.text: Any police officer may without an order from a Magistrate and without a warrant arrest any person who has been concerned in any cognizable offence, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made.
When a police officer arrests any person without warrant, he shall immediately communicate to the person arrested the full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested.
Whenever a person is arrested by a police officer, the police officer may search the person arrested and place in safe custody all articles other than necessary wearing apparel found upon him.
Whenever it is necessary to cause a woman to be searched, the search shall be made by another woman with strict regard to decency.
Police may apply for custody of accused for up to 15 days.
The Magistrate may authorize judicial custody for up to 15 days at a time.
Maximum detention: 90 days for offences punishable with death/life/10+ years, 60 days for other offences.
When a person is arrested, the police officer may take measurements including fingerprints, photographs, and other identifying particulars.
Every police officer making an arrest shall, without unnecessary delay, make a report of the arrest to the officer in charge of the police station.
A person arrested shall not be detained in custody for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable.
A police officer may release a person arrested on his executing a bond with or without sureties for his appearance before a Magistrate.
On completion of investigation, the police shall forward a report to the Magistrate.
Documents may be served through electronic means.
A Magistrate may take cognizance upon complaint, police report, or information.

sections.section_title: Jurisdiction in case of offences committed on journey
sections.text: When an offence is committed whilst the offender is in the course of performing a journey, the offence may be inquired into or tried by a Court through whose local jurisdiction the person or thing passed in the course of that journey.

When it is uncertain in which of several local areas an offence was committed, or where an offence is committed partly in one local area and partly in another, it may be inquired into or tried by a Court having jurisdiction over any of such local areas.
When an offence is committed while the offender is on a journey, it may be inquired into or tried by a Court through whose local jurisdiction the offender passed.

sections.section_title: High Court's power to order trial
sections.text: Whenever doubt arises as to the proper Court of jurisdiction, the High Court may determine in which Court the offence shall be inquired into or tried.

(1) Whenever it is made to appear to the High Court that an order under this section is expedient for the ends of justice, it may order that any particular case be transferred from one Criminal Court to another Criminal Court. (2) The High Court may act on the report of the lower Court or on the application of a party interested.

sections.section_title: Transfer of case on application of accused
sections.text: When a complaint is made or a case is pending, the accused may apply to the High Court for transfer of the case on the ground that a fair and impartial trial cannot be held in the Court where the case is pending.
A complaint may be made to a Magistrate regarding commission of an offence.

A Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence on complaint shall examine upon oath the complainant and the witnesses present, if any, and the substance of such examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed by the complainant and the witnesses, and also by the Magistrate.

If after considering the complaint and the evidence of the complainant and witnesses, the Magistrate is satisfied that there is sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall issue process for the appearance of the accused.

If after considering the complaint and the evidence of the complainant and witnesses, the Magistrate is of opinion that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall dismiss the complaint, recording briefly his reasons for so doing.

sections.section_title: Security for keeping peace in other cases
sections.text: When an Executive Magistrate receives information that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity or to do any wrongful act that may occasion a breach of the peace, the Magistrate may require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond for keeping the peace for such period, not exceeding one year, as the Magistrate thinks fit.
sections.chapter: IX — Security for Keeping the Peace

sections.text: (1) When any Magistrate acting under this Chapter requires a person to show cause, he shall make an order in writing setting forth the substance of the information received. (2) The Magistrate shall then inquire into the truth of the information and take such evidence as is necessary.
sections.chapter: IX — Security for Keeping the Peace

sections.text: If after inquiry the Magistrate is satisfied that it is necessary to require the person to execute a bond for keeping the peace, he shall pass an order requiring him to execute such bond for a sum proportionate to his means.
sections.chapter: IX — Security for Keeping the Peace

sections.section_title: Warrant in lieu of summons, or summons in lieu of warrant
sections.text: The Court may, in any case in which it is empowered to issue a summons for the appearance of any person, issue a warrant for his arrest instead of a summons, if after recording its reasons it is satisfied that such person will not attend voluntarily.
sections.chapter: IX — Security for Keeping the Peace

sections.section_title: Security for keeping the peace on conviction
sections.text: When a person is convicted of an offence involving a breach of the peace or of an offence likely to occasion a breach of the peace, the Court may, in addition to passing sentence, require him to execute a bond for keeping the peace for a period not exceeding three years.
sections.chapter: IX — Security for Keeping the Peace

sections.section_title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents
sections.text: A Magistrate of the First Class may order maintenance for wife, child, or parent unable to maintain themselves.
The Magistrate shall order maintenance at a monthly rate considering financial capacity and needs.
The Magistrate may order interim maintenance pending final determination.
On failure to pay, the Magistrate may issue a warrant for levying the amount.
The Magistrate may alter the maintenance order on change of circumstances.
Proceedings for maintenance under this Chapter may be taken against any person in any district where he resides or where he last resided, or where the wife resides.

A copy of the maintenance order shall be given to the person in whose favour it is made, and if the person ordered to pay fails without sufficient cause to comply with the order, the Magistrate may issue a warrant for levying the amount.
On proof of a change in the circumstances of the person receiving maintenance, the Magistrate may make such alteration in the allowance as he thinks fit.
If the person in whose favour a maintenance order is made remarries, the maintenance order shall be cancelled.
The Magistrate may order maintenance for legitimate or illegitimate children unable to maintain themselves.
Pending the final determination of the application, the Magistrate may order interim maintenance at such rate as may be deemed just.
The Magistrate may order maintenance from the date of the order, or if he thinks fit, from the date of the application.

In any proceeding under this Chapter, the evidence of the wife, child or parent shall be taken on oath and the Magistrate may, for reasons to be recorded, dispense with the attendance of the husband or father if satisfied that his presence is not necessary.

Proceedings under this Chapter may be held in camera if the Magistrate considers it necessary and the Magistrate may, for the purpose of enforcing attendance of any person, exercise all the powers of a Civil Court.

sections.section_title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger
sections.text: In cases where there is urgent nuisance or apprehended danger, any District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate may, by a written order, direct any person to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to certain property in his possession or under his management.
sections.chapter: XI — Maintenance of Public Order and Tranquillity

sections.text: Every information of a cognizable offence shall be reduced to writing, signed by the informant, and entered in a book.
When information is given to a police officer of the commission of a non-cognizable offence, he shall enter the substance of the information in a book and refer the informant to the Magistrate.
A police officer is bound to register an FIR on receiving information of a cognizable offence.
A police officer may register FIR regardless of place of occurrence.

The officer in charge of a police station shall maintain a diary of the investigation in such form as the State Government may prescribe, recording the day to day proceedings and the time at which information was received and the proceedings commenced and closed.

On the completion of the investigation, the officer in charge of the police station shall forward to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence a report in the prescribed form setting forth the facts and circumstances of the case and the names of the witnesses.

sections.section_title: Release of accused when evidence deficient
sections.text: If, upon investigation, it appears to the officer in charge of the police station that there is no sufficient evidence or reasonable ground to proceed against the accused, he shall release the accused, if in custody, on his executing a bond for appearance before the Magistrate when required.
Bail is release from custody on furnishing security. Bail is the rule, jail is the exception.
When arrested for a bailable offence, the person shall be released on bail.
A court may release on bail for non-bailable offences unless punishable with death or life imprisonment.
The court shall consider: nature of accusation, antecedents, flight risk, evidence tampering, witness intimidation.
No bail under NDPS, PMLA, UAPA unless court finds reasonable grounds accused is not guilty.
The court may impose conditions: surrender of passport, reporting to police, surety.
The accused shall execute a bail bond with or without sureties as the court may direct.
If investigation is not completed within 90 or 60 days, the accused has a right to default bail.
A person who apprehends arrest may apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for anticipatory bail.
A court may cancel bail if conditions are violated or the accused tampers with evidence.
An appeal lies against an order granting or refusing bail.

sections.section_title: Bail when cognizable offence listed in First Schedule
sections.text: When any person accused of a cognizable offence listed in column 3 of the First Schedule is arrested or detained, he shall be released on bail if there are no reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of such an offence.

sections.section_title: Bail in case of non-cognizable offence
sections.text: When any person accused of a non-cognizable offence is arrested or detained by a police officer, he shall be released on bail.

sections.section_title: Bail in case of bailable offence
sections.text: When any person accused of a bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant, he shall be released on bail by the police officer having custody.

When any person is detained in custody pending investigation, inquiry or trial, the total period of detention shall not exceed one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment prescribed for such offence.

sections.section_title: Bail not to be cancelled without notice
sections.text: A person who has been released on bail shall not be arrested and committed to custody without notice to the person or his surety of the application for cancellation of bail.

sections.section_title: Power to grant bail subject to conditions
sections.text: The Court may impose conditions while granting bail including conditions for surrender of passport, reporting to police, or not tampering with evidence.

Where a person is accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years or more, the Court may refuse bail if there are substantial grounds for believing that the accused would commit an offence while on bail.

When any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section.

sections.section_title: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest
sections.text: Where the High Court or the Court of Session grants anticipatory bail, it may impose such conditions as it thinks fit including a condition that the person shall not leave India without the permission of the Court.
The Court may pass orders to protect the safety of witnesses and ensure that they are not tampered with during the trial.

(1) Every charge shall be in writing and shall contain the statement of the offence with which the accused is charged. (2) If the law which creates the offence gives it any specific name, the offence may be described in the charge by that name only.

Every charge under this Sanhita shall state the offence with which the accused is charged, together with particulars of the time and place of the alleged offence and the person against whom it was committed.

No error in stating either the offence or the particulars required to be stated in the charge, and no omission to state the offence or those particulars, shall be regarded as material unless the accused was in fact misled by such error or omission.

(1) Any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time before judgment is pronounced. (2) Every alteration or addition shall be read and explained to the accused. (3) If the alteration or addition is such that proceeding immediately with the trial is likely to prejudice the accused, the Court may order a new trial or adjourn the trial.

sections.section_title: Recall of witnesses when charge altered
sections.text: Whenever a charge is altered or added to after the commencement of the trial, the prosecutor and the accused shall be allowed to recall or re-summon and examine any witness who may have been examined, unless the Court considers that the purpose of justice does not require it.
For every distinct offence of which any person is accused there shall be a separate charge, and every such charge shall be tried separately except as provided in sections 219, 220, 221 and 222.

sections.section_title: Joinder of charges of same kind
sections.text: When a person is accused of more offences than one of the same kind committed within a period of twelve months, he may be charged with and tried at one trial for any number of them not exceeding three.

sections.section_title: Trial for more than one offence
sections.text: If, in one series of acts so connected together as to form the same transaction, more offences than one are committed by the same person, he may be charged with and tried at one trial for every such offence.

sections.section_title: When offence proved is included in offence charged
sections.text: When a person is charged with an offence consisting of several particulars, and the proof shows that he committed a different offence but the one charged is a minor offence included in the major one, he may be convicted of the minor offence.
All trials before a Court of Session shall be conducted in accordance with this Chapter.
The trial in a Court of Session shall be conducted in accordance with the procedure specified in this Chapter.

When the accused appears or is brought before the Court in pursuance of a commitment of the case, the prosecutor shall open his case by describing the charge against the accused and stating the evidence by which he proposes to prove the guilt of the accused.

If after considering the record of the case and the documents submitted, the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons.

If after considering the record and documents and after hearing the submissions of both sides, the Judge is of opinion that there is ground for presuming that the accused has committed an offence, he shall frame in writing a charge against the accused.
If the accused pleads guilty, the Judge shall record the plea and may in his discretion convict the accused.
After the prosecution evidence is concluded, the accused shall be called upon to enter his defence and produce his evidence.

When the examination of the accused and the evidence for the defence are concluded, the prosecutor shall sum up his case and the accused or his pleader shall be entitled to reply. The Court shall then pronounce judgment.
If the accused is not convicted, the Judge shall record an order of acquittal.
The Court, after hearing the arguments, shall deliver judgment in open Court, specifying the offence of which the accused is convicted and the sentence or other order passed.
Every judgment shall contain the point for determination, the decision thereon, and the reasons for the decision.
The Court may order the accused to pay compensation to the victim for any loss or injury caused by the offence.
The Court may order payment of costs by the accused or the complainant in certain cases.
When a sentence of imprisonment is passed, the Court shall issue a warrant for the execution of the sentence.
The Court may pass any sentence authorized by law, but the sentence shall not exceed the maximum punishment provided for the offence.
The Court may suspend the execution of sentence pending an appeal.
When a person is convicted of two or more offences, the Court may order the sentences to run concurrently or consecutively.
The High Court may transfer any case from one Court subordinate to it to another Court for trial.
In a warrant-case instituted on a police report, the Magistrate shall follow the procedure specified in this Chapter.

(1) When the accused appears or is brought before a Magistrate, the Magistrate shall proceed to hear the complainant and take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution. (2) The Magistrate may, on the application of the prosecution, issue summons to any witness.

(1) If, after taking the evidence for the prosecution and examining the accused, the Magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall record an order of acquittal. (2) If the Magistrate finds the accused guilty, he shall pass sentence according to law.
When the proceedings have been instituted upon complaint, and on the day fixed for hearing of the case, the complainant is absent, the Magistrate may, in his discretion, acquit the accused.
Certain offences may be tried summarily by a Magistrate.
In a summons-case, the Magistrate shall, as soon as the accused appears, state the particulars of the offence to the accused and ask him whether he pleads guilty or claims trial.
If the accused pleads guilty, the Magistrate shall record the plea and may, in his discretion, convict him.
If, after the evidence of the complainant and the accused have been taken, the Magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall record an order of acquittal.
A complainant may, at any time before a final order is passed, withdraw his complaint. In such case, the Magistrate shall acquit the accused.

(1) A Chief Judicial Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class may try summarily any offence which is not punishable with death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term exceeding three years. (2) The Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, try any such case as a summons case.

In summary trials, the Magistrate shall record the substance of the evidence and the particulars of the finding and sentence. No judgment of a summary trial shall contain a detailed judgment exceeding the prescribed form.

(1) A person accused of an offence may file an application for plea bargaining in the Court in which the offence is pending for trial. (2) The application shall contain a brief description of the case and be accompanied by an affidavit stating that the accused has voluntarily accepted the plea offer.

(1) On receipt of an application under section 265, the Court shall issue notice to the Public Prosecutor and the complainant, if any, and fix a date for the hearing. (2) The Court shall satisfy itself that the application is voluntary and shall give the accused an opportunity to be heard.
An appeal lies from a conviction by a Magistrate to the Sessions Court.
An appeal lies from a Sessions Court conviction to the High Court.
An appeal lies to the Supreme Court in certain cases.
No appeal lies for petty offences where fine only is imposed.
The State may appeal against an order of acquittal.
The appellate court may admit new evidence if necessary.
The appellate court may reverse, alter, or confirm the judgment.

Any person convicted on a trial held by a Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge, or on a trial held by any other Court in which a sentence of imprisonment for more than seven years has been passed, may appeal to the High Court.
There shall be no appeal in cases where a Magistrate imposes a fine only not exceeding one thousand rupees, or where a sentence of imprisonment does not exceed three months.
The State Government may direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal to the High Court from an order of acquittal passed by any Court.

The appellate Court may in an appeal: (a) reverse the finding and sentence and acquit or discharge the accused, or order him to be re-tried, (b) alter the finding, or (c) alter the nature or the extent, or the nature and extent, of the sentence.
If the appellate Court considers that there is no sufficient ground for interfering, it may dismiss the appeal summarily.
If the appellant is in jail, he may present his appeal through the officer in charge of the jail.
The appellate Court may, if the accused is in confinement, direct that he be released on bail or on his own bond pending the disposal of the appeal.
The provisions of this Sanhita relating to bail shall be construed liberally.
Any court may summon any person as a witness at any stage of the proceedings.

(1) No Court shall take cognizance of an offence after the expiry of the period of limitation. (2) The period of limitation shall be: (a) six months for offences punishable with fine only; (b) one year for offences punishable with imprisonment not exceeding one year; (c) three years for offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding one year but not exceeding three years.

(1) The period of limitation shall commence on the date of the offence. (2) Where the commission of the offence was not known to the person aggrieved, it shall commence on the date on which it first became known to him.
The High Court may make any order to prevent abuse of process or secure ends of justice.
Nothing in this Sanhita shall limit the inherent powers of the High Court.

Nothing in this Sanhita shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
The High Court may make rules consistent with this Sanhita for carrying on proceedings before Criminal Courts.
The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is hereby repealed. Notwithstanding such repeal, any action taken under the repealed Code shall be deemed to have been taken under this Sanhita.
Where any Court is satisfied that a case pending before it involves a question as to the validity of any Act or Regulation, it shall refer the question to the High Court for decision.

The High Court may call for and examine the record of any proceeding before any inferior Criminal Court situate within its local jurisdiction for the purpose of satisfying itself as to the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order.

Any Sessions Judge may call for and examine the record of any proceeding before any Magistrate subordinate to him for the purpose of satisfying himself as to the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order.
When a case is referred for revision, the Magistrate whose order is challenged shall, if required, submit a written statement setting forth the grounds of his decision.

sections.section_title: Power of High Court to transfer cases
sections.text: The High Court may, on the application of any person interested, order that any particular case be transferred from one Criminal Court to another Criminal Court in the same State or from any Criminal Court to any other Criminal Court of equal or superior jurisdiction.
When a sentence of imprisonment is passed, the Court shall issue a warrant for the execution of such sentence to the officer in charge of the jail in which the prisoner is to be confined.
sections.chapter: XXXIII — Execution, Suspension, Remission and Commutation of Sentences

sections.text: When an appeal is presented, the Appellate Court may, for reasons to be recorded, suspend the execution of the sentence pending the appeal.
sections.chapter: XXXIII — Execution, Suspension, Remission and Commutation of Sentences

sections.text: The appropriate Government may, without the consent of the person sentenced, remit or commute any sentence, subject to conditions as may be specified.
sections.chapter: XXXIII — Execution, Suspension, Remission and Commutation of Sentences

sections.text: When any person is arrested without warrant and is prepared to give bail, the officer in charge of the police station shall release him on bail if the offence is bailable.
sections.chapter: XXXIV — Provisions as to Bail and Bonds

sections.text: When any person is arrested and is prepared to give bail, the Magistrate before whom he is produced shall release him on bail if the offence is bailable.
sections.chapter: XXXIV — Provisions as to Bail and Bonds

sections.section_title: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest
sections.text: When any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section; and that Court may, if it thinks fit, direct that in the event of such arrest, he shall be released on bail.
sections.chapter: XXXIV — Provisions as to Bail and Bonds

sections.text: (1) The amount of every bond executed under this Sanhita shall be fixed with due regard to the circumstances of the case and shall not be excessive. (2) The Court may accept the bond with or without sureties as it thinks fit. (3) A bond may be taken from any person who is present or from a surety.
sections.chapter: XXXIV — Provisions as to Bail and Bonds

sections.section_title: Public servants not to be compelled to disclose communications
sections.text: No public servant shall be compelled to disclose any communication made to him in official confidence, except with the permission of the officer to whom he is subordinate, if the public servant considers that such communication would be injurious to the public interest.
